BPM Justification: The Standard explicitly names "business processes" as one of the dimensions data should be tied to, which is a genuine, if modest, process-data-architecture decision rather than pure accounting policy.

This is a scoping step for an accounting exercise (which categories to measure), not a process design or modeling decision - the value-chain description here is a reporting-boundary artifact, not a process model.

Writing a data-reporting clause into an outsourcing contract is a concrete governance mechanism for controlling and measuring an outsourced activity, which is a real, if narrow, process-governance lever.
This is a pure accounting-consistency rule for comparing inventories over time after a corporate restructuring - there's no process design, modeling, or execution content here at all.

A five-step sequential method for calculating something is a generic project/workflow structuring technique applied here to GHG accounting; there's a loose process-step framing but it isn't a business process in the organizational sense.

Classifying emission sources by combustion/process/fugitive type is a measurement-methodology step; the UTC case is a good cautionary example but the underlying action (categorize before calculating) isn't itself a process-design decision.

Choosing where calculation happens (facility vs. corporate) is a real data-flow architecture decision, and the Standard explicitly ties the choice to process complexity and uniformity across sites, which is a genuinely BPM-adjacent design question.

Widening the scope of an existing operational/quality/reporting process to cover a new concern instead of building a parallel one is a direct process-integration decision, and it's the most repeated, best-evidenced lesson in the whole document across four separate case studies.

Standing up a cross-functional team to own a new reporting obligation is a familiar BPM governance pattern (process ownership spanning functions), but it's also just good general program-management practice independent of BPM.

A formal feedback loop from review findings back to a process owner is a recognizable BPM pattern (monitoring feeding back into redesign/correction), made explicit here as a numbered step in the Standard's own quality-management cycle.
Breaking a reported number down by cause is good reporting/analysis practice generally, applied here to emissions changes specifically, but it doesn't touch how any process is modeled or executed.

Securing leadership buy-in before a change initiative is standard change-management advice that applies to literally any corporate-wide target, with nothing BPM-specific about it beyond the target happening to be about emissions.

Matching a target's metric to the level of decision-making that can actually act on it is a genuine process-ownership insight, directly analogous to assigning the right KPI to the right role in a process hierarchy, and the Shell case study makes the mechanism explicit (production, design, and operator decisions are three different levers).
